title: Function, domain, range, independent and dependent variable
body: A function maps each input value in its domain to exactly one output value in its range; the input variable is independent and the output variable is dependent.
ced_evidence: 1.1.A.1 "each input value is mapped to exactly one output value"

title: Equal functions
body: Two functions f and g are equal if they have the same domain and f(a)=g(a) for every input a in that domain.
ced_evidence: 1.1.A.1 "Two functions, f and g, are equal if they have the same domain"

title: Image and preimage
body: The image of an input value is the single output the function rule yields, and the preimage of an output value is the set of inputs that yield it.
ced_evidence: 1.1.A.2 "The image of an input value is the single output value"; 1.12.A.5

title: Increasing function over an interval
body: a<b \Rightarrow f(a)<f(b)\text{ for all }a,b\text{ in the interval}
ced_evidence: 1.1.A.3 "if a < b, then f(a) < f(b)"

title: Decreasing function over an interval
body: a<b \Rightarrow f(a)>f(b)\text{ for all }a,b\text{ in the interval}
ced_evidence: 1.1.A.4 "if a < b, then f(a) > f(b)"

title: Concave up and concave down
body: A graph is concave up where the rate of change is increasing and concave down where the rate of change is decreasing.
ced_evidence: 1.1.B.3 and 1.1.B.4 "concave up on intervals in which the rate of change is increasing"

title: Zero of a function
body: A zero is an input value whose output is zero, where the graph intersects the x-axis.
ced_evidence: 1.1.B.5 "The corresponding input values are said to be zeros of the function"

title: Average rate of change over [a, b]
body: \frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}
caution: State it as the constant rate that yields the same change in output as the function over the interval, and as the slope of the secant line.
ced_evidence: 1.2.A.1 "ratio of the change in the output values to the change in input values"; 1.3.A.3

title: Average rate of change as secant slope
body: The average rate of change of f over [a, b] is the slope of the secant line from (a, f(a)) to (b, f(b)).
ced_evidence: 1.3.A.3 "the slope of the secant line"

title: Rate of change at a point
body: The rate of change at a point is approximated by average rates of change over small intervals containing the point, and two such rates can be compared this way.
ced_evidence: 1.2.A.2 and 1.2.A.3 "approximated by the average rates of change of the function over small intervals"

title: Sign of a rate of change
body: A positive rate of change means both quantities increase or decrease together, while a negative rate of change means that as one increases the other decreases.

title: Average rates of change for linear and quadratic functions
body: Linear functions have a constant average rate of change over any equal-length intervals (changing at rate zero), while for quadratics the average rates over consecutive equal-length intervals follow a linear function (changing at a constant rate).

title: Concavity from changing average rates of change
body: If average rates of change over equal-length intervals are increasing the graph is concave up, and if they are decreasing it is concave down.
ced_evidence: 1.3.B.3 "the graph of the function is concave up"

title: Polynomial function in standard form
body: p(x)=a_n x^n+a_{n-1}x^{n-1}+a_{n-2}x^{n-2}+\cdots+a_2x^2+a_1x+a_0,\quad a_n\neq 0,\ n\text{ a positive integer}

title: Degree, leading term, leading coefficient
body: For a polynomial of the form above, n is the degree, a_n x^n is the leading term, and a_n is the leading coefficient.
ced_evidence: 1.4.A.1 "The polynomial has degree n, the leading term is a_n x^n"

title: Local and global extrema
body: A local maximum or minimum occurs where a polynomial switches between increasing and decreasing (or at an included endpoint), and it is global if it is greater (maximum) or less (minimum) than all other output values.
ced_evidence: 1.4.A.2 "local, or relative, maximum or minimum"

title: Extrema between zeros
body: Between every two distinct real zeros of a nonconstant polynomial function there is at least one input value giving a local maximum or local minimum.
ced_evidence: 1.4.A.3 "Between every two distinct real zeros"

title: Even-degree polynomials and global extrema
body: A polynomial of even degree has either a global maximum or a global minimum, and for a quadratic it occurs at the vertex.
ced_evidence: 1.4.A.4 "even degree has either a global maximum or a global minimum"

title: Point of inflection
body: A point of inflection of a polynomial occurs at an input where the rate of change switches between increasing and decreasing, i.e., where the graph changes concavity.
ced_evidence: 1.4.A.5 "Points of inflection of a polynomial function occur at input values"

title: Zeros and linear factors
body: If a is a zero of p (a root of p(x)=0), then for real a the expression (x-a) is a linear factor of p if and only if a is a zero, and a real zero gives an x-intercept at (a, 0).
ced_evidence: 1.5.A.1 "(x - a) is a linear factor of p if and only if a is a zero of p"; 1.5.A.3

title: Multiplicity of a zero
body: If a linear factor (x-a) is repeated n times, the corresponding zero has multiplicity n, and a degree-n polynomial has exactly n complex zeros counting multiplicities.
ced_evidence: 1.5.A.2 "has a multiplicity n"

title: Non-real zeros come in conjugate pairs
body: If a+bi is a non-real zero of a polynomial function p, then its conjugate a−bi is also a zero of p.
ced_evidence: 1.5.A.4 "its conjugate a − bi is also a zero of p"

title: Zeros as endpoints of inequality intervals
body: Real zeros of a polynomial can be endpoints of the intervals that satisfy polynomial inequalities.
ced_evidence: 1.5.A.3 "real zeros of a polynomial can be endpoints for intervals satisfying polynomial inequalities"

title: Even-multiplicity zeros
body: If a real zero has even multiplicity, the output signs are the same for inputs near x=a and the graph is tangent to the x-axis at x=a.
ced_evidence: 1.5.A.5 "the graph will be tangent to the x-axis at x = a"

title: Degree from successive differences
body: The degree of a polynomial equals the least n for which the successive nth differences of outputs over equal-interval inputs are constant.
ced_evidence: 1.5.A.6 "least value n for which the successive nth differences are constant"

title: Even function
body: f(-x)=f(x)
caution: Also state that the graph is symmetric over the line x=0; p(x)=a_n x^n with n even is an even function.
ced_evidence: 1.5.B.1 "analytically has the property f(-x) = f(x)"

title: Odd function
caution: Also state that the graph is symmetric about the point (0, 0); p(x)=a_n x^n with n odd is an odd function.
ced_evidence: 1.5.B.2 "analytically has the property f(-x) = -f(x)"

title: End behavior limit notation for polynomials
body: \lim_{x\to\infty}p(x)=\pm\infty\quad\text{and}\quad\lim_{x\to-\infty}p(x)=\pm\infty
ced_evidence: 1.6.A.1 and 1.6.A.2 "lim p(x) = ∞ or lim p(x) = -∞"

title: Leading term determines polynomial end behavior
body: The degree and sign of the leading term determine the end behavior, because for inputs of large magnitude the leading term dominates all lower-degree terms.
ced_evidence: 1.6.A.3 "the values of the leading term dominate the values of all lower-degree terms"

title: Rational function
body: A rational function is analytically represented as a quotient of two polynomial functions.
ced_evidence: 1.7.A.1 "a quotient of two polynomial functions"

title: Rational end behavior: compare leading terms
body: End behavior of a rational function comes from the quotient of the leading terms, in three cases of which polynomial dominates.

items.label: Numerator dominates
items.meaning: Quotient of leading terms is a nonconstant polynomial; the function has that polynomial's end behavior, and a linear quotient gives a slant asymptote parallel to that line.

items.label: Neither dominates
items.meaning: Quotient of leading terms is a constant, which gives the horizontal asymptote.

items.label: Denominator dominates
items.meaning: Quotient is a constant over a nonconstant polynomial, giving a horizontal asymptote at y=0.

expands_to.means: Bigger exponent On Bottom, asymptote y = 0
Bigger exponent On Top, no horizontal asymptote
Exponents Are The Same, divide the leading coefficients

hooks.when_to_use: To quickly recall which of the three degree-comparison cases applies.
hooks.caution: In your answer, justify with the CED's reasoning: the leading terms dominate for large inputs, so use the quotient of the leading terms. When the top is bigger, give the polynomial end behavior or slant asymptote.

title: Horizontal asymptote limit notation
body: \lim_{x\to\infty}r(x)=b\quad\text{or}\quad\lim_{x\to-\infty}r(x)=b
ced_evidence: 1.7.A.6 "horizontal asymptote at y = b"

title: Zeros of a rational function
body: The real zeros of a rational function correspond to the real zeros of the numerator that lie in its domain.
ced_evidence: 1.8.A.1 "correspond to the real zeros of the numerator"

title: Rational inequalities: endpoints and asymptotes
body: The real zeros of both the numerator and denominator of r are endpoints or asymptotes for the intervals satisfying r(x) ≥ 0 or r(x) ≤ 0.
ced_evidence: 1.8.A.2 "endpoints or asymptotes for intervals satisfying the rational function inequalities"

title: Vertical asymptote condition
body: A rational function has a vertical asymptote at x=a if a is a real zero of the denominator and not of the numerator, or if a has greater multiplicity in the denominator than in the numerator.
ced_evidence: 1.9.A.1 "the graph of the rational function has a vertical asymptote at x = a"

title: Vertical asymptote limit notation
body: \lim_{x\to a^{+}}r(x)=\pm\infty\quad\text{and}\quad\lim_{x\to a^{-}}r(x)=\pm\infty
caution: Describe each side separately: near a the denominator is arbitrarily close to zero, so the outputs increase or decrease without bound.
ced_evidence: 1.9.A.2 "lim r(x) = ∞ or lim r(x) = -∞"

title: Hole condition
body: A rational function has a hole at an input if the multiplicity of that real zero in the numerator is greater than or equal to its multiplicity in the denominator.
ced_evidence: 1.10.A.1 "greater than or equal to its multiplicity in the denominator"

title: Location of a hole
body: \lim_{x\to c}r(x)=L\ \Rightarrow\ \text{hole at }(c,L)
caution: Justify using output values for inputs sufficiently close to c; the left, right, and two-sided limits are all equal to L.
ced_evidence: 1.10.A.2 "the hole is located at the point with coordinates (c, L)"

title: Factored form vs. standard form
body: Factored form readily reveals real zeros, x-intercepts, asymptotes, holes, domain, and range, while standard form reveals end behavior.

title: Polynomial long division identity
body: f(x)=g(x)\,q(x)+r(x),\quad \deg r<\deg g
caution: Here q is the quotient and r is the remainder; the quotient gives the slant asymptote equation of a rational function.

title: Binomial theorem uses a row of Pascal's Triangle
body: Expanding (a+b)^n, including (x+c)^n, uses the entries in a single row of Pascal's Triangle.
ced_evidence: 1.11.C.1 "entries in a single row of Pascal's Triangle"

title: Additive and multiplicative transformations
body: The four basic transformation forms of g in terms of f, and their effect on the graph of f.

items.label: g(x)=f(x)+k
items.meaning: Vertical translation by k units.

items.label: g(x)=f(x+h)
items.meaning: Horizontal translation by −h units.

items.label: g(x)=a·f(x), a≠0
items.meaning: Vertical dilation by factor |a|; reflection over the x-axis if a<0.

items.label: g(x)=f(bx), b≠0
items.meaning: Horizontal dilation by factor 1/|b|; reflection over the y-axis if b<0.

hooks.hook_text: Inside changes are backwards and horizontal; outside changes are as expected and vertical.

expands_to.means: horizontal effect, opposite of what the sign suggests (−h shift, 1/b dilation)

hooks.when_to_use: To keep the direction of horizontal versus vertical transformations straight.
hooks.caution: In your answer, state the CED's exact effects: a horizontal translation by −h units, a horizontal dilation by factor 1/|b|, and a reflection when the sign is negative.

title: Combined transformations and changed domain/range
body: Transformations can be combined, mapping the preimage points to image points, and the domain and range of the transformed function may differ from those of the parent function.

title: Choosing a function type for a model
body: Match the data or scenario characteristic to the function type that models it.

items.label: Linear
items.meaning: Roughly constant rates of change.

items.label: Quadratic
items.meaning: Roughly linear rates of change, or roughly symmetric data with a unique maximum or minimum; also area or two-dimensional contexts.

items.label: Cubic
items.meaning: Volume or three-dimensional contexts.

items.label: Polynomial (general)
items.meaning: Multiple real zeros or multiple maxima or minima; degree n if the nth differences are roughly constant and nonzero.

items.label: Piecewise-defined
items.meaning: Different characteristics over different, nonoverlapping domain intervals.

title: Points determine polynomial degree
body: A polynomial function of degree n or less can model a graph of n+1 points with distinct input values.
ced_evidence: 1.13.A.6 "degree n or less can be used to model a graph of n + 1 points"

title: Model assumptions and restrictions
body: A model may carry assumptions and restrictions that should be articulated.

items.label: Consistency assumptions
items.meaning: Assumptions about what is consistent in the model.

items.label: Covariation assumptions
items.meaning: Assumptions about how quantities change together.

items.label: Domain restrictions
items.meaning: Based on mathematical clues, contextual clues, or extreme values in the data set.

items.label: Range restrictions
items.meaning: Such as rounding values, based on mathematical clues, contextual clues, or extreme values.

title: Ways to construct a function model
body: Models can be built from restrictions, transformations of a parent function, regressions, or combined techniques.

items.label: Restrictions
items.meaning: Built from restrictions in a mathematical or contextual scenario.

items.label: Transformations
items.meaning: Transformations of the parent function.

items.label: Regression
items.meaning: Technology-based linear, quadratic, cubic, and quartic regressions.

items.label: Piecewise
items.meaning: A combination of modeling techniques.

title: Inversely proportional quantities suggest rational models
body: Data or scenarios with inversely proportional quantities, such as force versus squared distance, can often be modeled by rational functions.
ced_evidence: 1.14.B.1 "quantities that are inversely proportional can often be modeled by rational functions"

title: Using a model and units
body: A model can answer questions and predict values, rates of change, average rates of change, and changing rates of change, with units of measure extracted or inferred from the context.
ced_evidence: 1.14.C.1 "Appropriate units of measure should be extracted or inferred from the given context"
